one_liner: AVX2/AVX-512 C implementation of a xorshift128+-style generator, about 1.6-2.5x the throughput of scalar xorshift128+.
what_it_does: A small C99 library (two .c files plus headers) that runs four (AVX2) or eight (AVX-512) independent xorshift128+-style lanes in one vector register, returning 256 or 512 random bits per call (avx_xorshift128plus / avx512_xorshift128plus). It also ships a jump function for making per-thread streams and a vectorized Fisher-Yates shuffle of uint32 arrays (avx_xorshift128plus_shuffle32). The API takes raw __m256i/__m512i values and an explicit key struct, so it is not a drop-in replacement for any std <random> engine.
how_it_is_fast: SIMD lanes: the xorshift/shift/add recurrence is expressed with 64-bit vector shifts, XORs and adds, so one call produces 4 or 8 64-bit outputs. Lanes are seeded 2^64 steps apart with the xorshift128+ jump polynomial. The 'two' benchmark variants interleave two independent keys to hide the dependency-chain latency. The shuffle maps random words into ranges with Lemire's multiply-shift bounded-integer method (slightly biased) rather than division or rejection.
when_to_use: Filling large buffers with non-cryptographic random bits on x86-64 with AVX2 (Haswell+) or AVX-512, where generator throughput is the bottleneck
Synthetic test data, hashing salts, randomized benchmarks or Monte Carlo prototypes where statistical quality is not critical
Bulk shuffles of uint32 arrays where a tiny modulo bias (order of n/2^32) is acceptable
Code that already works in __m256i/__m512i registers and wants random vectors without a scalar-to-vector round trip
when_not_to_use: Anything that needs the real xorshift128+ sequence or its stated period: the AVX2 and AVX-512 step functions shift the second state word (part2) where Vigna's reference shifts the first (part1), so part1 is never read and each lane's state is effectively one 64-bit word (see gotchas); output does not match the scalar generator
Simulations where quality matters: the README says xorshift128+ fails BigCrush and should not be used alone when quality matters, and the SIMD variant has not been separately tested
Non-x86 targets or pre-Haswell CPUs: the code needs AVX2 intrinsics, with no fallback or runtime dispatch
Cryptography or security tokens: it is not a CSPRNG
Workloads dominated by memory traffic, such as shuffling large arrays; the README notes the gain shrinks there

integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler with AVX2 intrinsics (Makefile uses -std=c99 -O3 -mavx2 -march=native); AVX-512 path compiled only when __AVX512F__ is defined
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 required; AVX-512F optional
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe per key; header says each thread should have its own key (use avx_xorshift128plus_jump to derive one)

gotchas: State-update bug read from src/simdxorshift128plus.c: avx_xorshift128plus does s1 = part2 ^ (part2 << 23) after part1 = part2, while the scalar reference (src/xorshift128plus.c) computes s1 = old part1 ^ (old part1 << 23). The vector generator therefore drops half its state and produces a different sequence from the scalar baseline it is benchmarked against; avx512_xorshift128plus has the same code. Found by source inspection; no issue or fix was found
Functions live in separate .c files; the author's blog notes the first measurements were slow because they did not inline, so build with -flto or move them into a header
Seeds must be non-zero and the library does not check them; the AVX-512 init still carries a 'todo: fix this so that the init is correct' comment, and there is no AVX-512 jump function
The README's 'used by ClickHouse' claim is stale: current ClickHouse master FunctionsRandom.cpp uses a vectorized linear congruential generator and no xorshift code
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Randen or Squares only when you need raw non-cryptographic random bits on AVX2 hardware and quality is not a concern. Romu offers comparable speed with a scalar API. Randen is the choice when you need backtracking resistance, and Randompack when you need tested distributions. Given the state-update bug, a vectorized PCG or xoshiro is usually the safer choice for the same purpose.
verified_claims_summary: The author's fillarray benchmark (rdtsc, best of 50 runs) filled an array of 32-bit values on an unnamed Skylake-X with an unnamed compiler at -O3 -march=native -flto. Scalar xorshift128+ took 3.63 cycles/value, AVX2 2.21, two interleaved AVX2 keys 1.88 and two AVX-512 keys 1.47, about 2.5x (derived from page data). The current benchmark source uses 50,000 values, not the 5,000 the README states, and the timed SIMD code computes a different recurrence from the scalar baseline.
status_note: Abandoned since July 2020, but Apache-2.0 and a few hundred lines, so easy to vendor; whoever vendors it should fix the part1/part2 state update first.
